paragraphs.context: they would take their guns and go off into the woods
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Gregg and his sons love hunting more than anything. They go every Saturday, even eight-year-old Philip.
paragraphs.simple: Mr Gregg and his two boys liked one thing more than all other things. They liked to go hunting. Every Saturday morning they took their guns and went into the woods. They looked for animals and birds to shoot. Even Philip had his own gun. He was only eight years old.

paragraphs.context: I would do my best to talk them out of it
paragraphs.mainIdea: The girl hates hunting and tries to stop the Greggs. They do not listen to her.
paragraphs.simple: I hate hunting. I cannot bear it. I think it is wrong. Men and boys should not kill animals just for fun. So I tried to stop Philip and William. Each time I went to their farm, I tried hard to make them stop. But they only laughed at me.

paragraphs.context: I had been telling myself that I would never put the Magic Finger
paragraphs.mainIdea: For a long time the girl has told herself not to use the Magic Finger again. This is because of what happened to Mrs Winter.
paragraphs.simple: For many months I had told myself the same thing. I would never use the Magic Finger on anyone again. This was because of what happened to my teacher, old Mrs Winter.

paragraphs.context: Will you be so kind as to tell me what you find so madly funny
paragraphs.mainIdea: The class laughs loudly. Mrs Winter asks in a very polite way why they are laughing.
paragraphs.simple: All the class began to laugh very loudly. Then Mrs Winter spoke. She said, 'Please tell me what is so funny. Tell me, all of you.' She used very polite words.

paragraphs.context: I cannot begin to tell you what happened after that
paragraphs.mainIdea: The girl cannot tell all that happened next. Mrs Winter is not well, and she never will be.
paragraphs.simple: I cannot tell you all that happened next. Maybe you want to know if Mrs Winter is well again now. She is not. She will never be well again.

paragraphs.context: Mr Gregg and Philip and William went out hunting once again
paragraphs.mainIdea: That afternoon the Greggs go hunting again. This time they look for wild ducks.
paragraphs.simple: That same afternoon Mr Gregg, Philip and William went hunting again. It was the day I put the Magic Finger on the Gregg family. This time they went after wild ducks. So they walked towards the lake.

paragraphs.context: He stopped and looked up. The night was very still
paragraphs.mainIdea: At night Mr Gregg sees the four ducks flying around his house.
paragraphs.simple: Mr Gregg stopped and looked up. The night was very quiet. A thin yellow moon was over the trees on the hill. The sky was full of stars. Then he heard wings flying low above his head. He saw the four ducks. They were dark against the sky and flew very close together. They were going around and around the house.

paragraphs.context: there below them, in their own garden, they saw four enormous wild ducks
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Greggs see four very big ducks in their garden. The ducks have arms like men.
paragraphs.simple: The family all looked down. In their own garden they saw four very big wild ducks. The ducks were as big as men. Also, they had long arms like men, not wings.

paragraphs.context: Every time you try to get your teeth into it, it just pushes away
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is hard to eat apples with no hands. They only get a few small bites, and then they go to sleep in the nest.
paragraphs.simple: Eating an apple is not easy when you cannot hold it in your hands. Each time you try to bite it, it moves away. At last they each got a few small bites. Then it began to get dark. So they all flew back to the nest and lay down to sleep.

paragraphs.context: Mr and Mrs Gregg and Philip and William were trying to get some sleep
paragraphs.mainIdea: The night in the nest is very bad. There is wind and rain, and everyone gets wet.
paragraphs.simple: That night the Greggs tried to sleep in the high nest. A great wind began to blow. The tree rocked from side to side. Everyone was afraid that the nest would fall down, even Mr Gregg. Then came the rain. It rained and rained. Water ran into the nest, and they all got as wet as could be. It was a bad, bad night.

paragraphs.context: the black that was before their eyes turned to blue, to green, to red
paragraphs.mainIdea: The colours change, and then the Greggs are suddenly in their own garden. Everything is normal again.
paragraphs.simple: Then the black in front of their eyes turned to blue, then green, then red, and then gold. And suddenly there they were. They were standing in lovely bright sun in their own garden, near their own house. Everything was back to normal.

paragraphs.context: and I must admit I was expecting the worst
paragraphs.mainIdea: The girl goes to the Greggs' garden. She expects the worst.
paragraphs.simple: About half an hour later I walked into the Greggs' garden. I had come to see how things were going. I must say that I expected the worst. I stopped at the gate and stared. It was a strange thing to see.

paragraphs.context: placing beautiful flowers upon sixteen tiny mounds of soil which I learned later
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs Gregg puts flowers on small graves. They are the graves of the ducks that were shot the day before.
paragraphs.simple: In another corner Mrs Gregg was putting beautiful flowers on sixteen small piles of earth. Later I learned that these were the graves of the ducks. They were the ducks that had been shot the day before.

paragraphs.context: They were surrounded by ducks, doves, pigeons, sparrows, robins, larks, and many other kinds
paragraphs.mainIdea: Philip and William feed barley to many kinds of birds in the yard.
paragraphs.simple: In the middle of the yard stood Philip and William. A sack of their father's best barley was beside them. Ducks, doves, pigeons, sparrows, robins, larks and many other kinds that I did not know were all around them. The boys were throwing barley by the handful, and the birds were eating it.

paragraphs.context: In honour of my feathered friends, I have changed it from Gregg to Egg
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Gregg says his name is not Gregg now. It is Egg, for his friends the birds.
paragraphs.simple: Mr Gregg put down his hammer and looked at me. He said, 'My name is not Gregg any more. To show respect for my friends the birds, I have changed it from Gregg to Egg.'

paragraphs.context: They’re shooting mad, those Coopers are, the whole family
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Egg says that the Coopers love shooting very much. The whole family is like that.
paragraphs.simple: 'That will be Jim Cooper,' Mr Egg said. 'He is with his three boys. Those Coopers love shooting very much. The whole family is the same.'

paragraphs.context: very good at making the sticks stick together
paragraphs.mainIdea: The same sound is two words. Sticks are small pieces of wood, and stick means they stay joined.
paragraphs.simple: The nest was getting bigger. Mr Gregg was very good at making the little pieces of wood hold on to each other.

paragraphs.context: long black whiskers, just like the ones you see
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hairs like a cat's start growing on the teacher's face. She is turning into a cat-kind of person.
paragraphs.simple: Long black hairs began to grow out of Mrs Winter's face. They were like the hairs on a cat, but much bigger. They grew so fast that they reached her ears.

paragraphs.context: he had a pair of duck's wings instead
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Gregg is no longer an ordinary man. Where his arms were, he now has the wings of a duck.
paragraphs.simple: His arms were gone. In their place he had two wings, like a duck.

paragraphs.context: now we are going to allow each other to shoot
paragraphs.mainIdea: The duck says the ducks will now shoot the people, just as the people shot ducks.
paragraphs.simple: The duck says that sounds fine. Now the ducks are going to let each other shoot Mr Gregg and his family.

sentences.context: Now the one thing that Mr Gregg and his two boys loved to do more than anything else was to go hunting
sentences.simple: Mr Gregg and his boys liked hunting more than all other things.
sentences.grammar: 'that Mr Gregg and his two boys loved to do' is a relative clause that tells which thing; 'was to go hunting' says what the thing was.

sentences.context: Every time I went over to their farm I would do my best to talk them out of it
sentences.simple: Each time I went to their farm, I tried hard to make them stop hunting.
sentences.grammar: 'would + verb' tells about something that happened again and again in the past; 'do my best to + verb' means try hard.

sentences.context: It doesn’t seem right to me that men and boys should kill animals just for the fun they get out of it
sentences.simple: I think it is wrong for men and boys to kill animals just for fun.
sentences.grammar: 'should kill' gives an opinion about what people do; 'the fun they get out of it' is a relative clause with 'that' left out.

sentences.context: Mr Gregg told me to go home and mind my own P’s and Q’s
sentences.simple: Mr Gregg told me to go home and take care how I behave.
sentences.grammar: 'told + person + to + verb' is how we report an order.

sentences.context: I did something I never meant to do
sentences.simple: I did something that I did not want to do.
sentences.grammar: 'something I never meant to do' is a relative clause with 'that' left out; 'never meant to' means did not plan to.

sentences.context: For months I had been telling myself that I would never put the Magic Finger upon anyone again
sentences.simple: For many months I had said to myself that I would not use the Magic Finger again.
sentences.grammar: 'had been telling' shows an action that went on for some time before a later past time; 'would never' is a promise for the future, told from the past.

sentences.context: Will you be so kind as to tell me what you find so madly funny
sentences.simple: Please tell me what you think is so funny.
sentences.grammar: 'Will you be so kind as to + verb' is a very polite way to ask; 'what you find so madly funny' is a noun clause.

sentences.context: we saw that she had grown a tail as well
sentences.simple: We saw that a tail had come out on her too.
sentences.grammar: 'had grown' is the past perfect: the tail grew before the moment we saw it; 'as well' means also.

sentences.context: if any of you are wondering whether Mrs Winter is quite all right again now
sentences.simple: Maybe you want to know if Mrs Winter is well again now.
sentences.grammar: 'are wondering whether ...' is present continuous with an indirect question; 'whether' means 'if'.

sentences.context: The Magic Finger is something I have been able to do all my life
sentences.simple: I have been able to use the Magic Finger for all my life.
sentences.grammar: 'have been able to' is the present perfect of 'can' (for all my life until now); 'something I have been able to do' is a relative clause with 'that' left out.

sentences.context: there was no taking it off again
sentences.simple: It was not possible to take it off again.
sentences.grammar: 'There is no + -ing word' means it is not possible to do that.

sentences.context: He was beside himself with joy
sentences.simple: He was extremely happy.
sentences.grammar: 'be beside oneself with + feeling' is an idiom: the feeling is so strong that the person cannot control it; 'himself' means Mr Gregg.

sentences.context: What on earth are they doing
sentences.simple: What are they doing? He is very surprised.
sentences.grammar: 'on earth' after a question word makes the question stronger and shows surprise.

sentences.context: It’s getting too dark to see
sentences.simple: It is becoming too dark for us to see.
sentences.grammar: 'getting + adjective' means becoming; 'too + adjective + to + verb' means too much for something to be possible.

sentences.context: He was about to put out a hand for his watch, to see the time
sentences.simple: He was going to put out a hand for his watch so that he could see the time.
sentences.grammar: 'was about to + verb' means he was just going to do it; 'to see the time' tells the purpose.

sentences.context: He lay still, wondering what was up
sentences.simple: He lay without moving and asked himself what was wrong.
sentences.grammar: 'wondering ...' is a participle phrase that shows two things happening together; 'what was up' means what was wrong.

sentences.context: He was maybe as tall as the seat of a chair, but no taller
sentences.simple: He was about as tall as the seat of a chair, and not taller.
sentences.grammar: 'as tall as' says two heights are the same; 'no taller' means not any taller.

sentences.context: But before she could say another word, Philip and William had flown right out the window
sentences.simple: Before she could say more, Philip and William had already flown out of the window.
sentences.grammar: 'before she could say ...' is a time clause; 'had flown' is the past perfect and shows it was already done.

sentences.context: Mr Gregg was very good at making the sticks stick together
sentences.simple: Mr Gregg was very good at making sticks stay together.
sentences.grammar: 'good at' is followed by the '-ing' form ('making').

sentences.context: But to eat an apple without holding it in your hands is not at all easy
sentences.simple: It is not easy to eat an apple when you cannot hold it in your hands.
sentences.grammar: The subject is 'to eat an apple without holding it in your hands'; 'without + -ing' means not doing something; 'not at all' makes 'not' stronger.

sentences.context: It must have been at about this time that I, back in my own house, picked up the telephone
sentences.simple: I am sure it was about this time that I picked up the telephone at my own house.
sentences.grammar: 'must have been' means I am sure it was so in the past; 'It was ... that ...' puts the focus on the time.

sentences.context: Just because we have wings, we don’t have to eat bird food
sentences.simple: We have wings. But that does not mean that we must eat bird food.
sentences.grammar: 'Just because ...' gives a reason, but the second part says it is not enough; 'don't have to' means it is not needed.

sentences.context: And now we are going to allow each other to shoot you
sentences.simple: And now we will let each other shoot you.
sentences.grammar: 'allow + person + to + verb' means to let someone do something; 'each other' means each one allows the other.

sentences.context: I would have loved to have seen Mr Gregg’s face just then
sentences.simple: I wish I could have seen Mr Gregg's face at that time.
sentences.grammar: 'would have loved to have seen' shows a wish about the past that did not come true.

sentences.context: I’ll never shoot another duck as long as I live
sentences.simple: I will never shoot another duck for all my life.
sentences.grammar: 'as long as I live' means for all the time I am alive; after 'as long as' we use the present tense ('live') for the future.

sentences.context: And never again need you be afraid of me or my family
sentences.simple: You will never need to be afraid of me or my family again.
sentences.grammar: Inversion: after 'never again' at the start, the verb comes before the subject ('need you be' instead of 'you need be').

sentences.context: They seemed to have gone completely dotty, all four of them
sentences.simple: It seemed that all four of them had gone completely mad.
sentences.grammar: 'seem to have + past participle' says that something seems to have happened before now.

sentences.context: Oh, we will be pecked to bits by those dirty great ducks
sentences.simple: Oh, those big dirty ducks will bite us into little pieces!
sentences.grammar: 'will be pecked' is the future passive (will be + past participle); 'by those ... ducks' says who does it; 'to bits' means into small pieces.

sentences.context: I shall now tell you what those things were
sentences.simple: Now I will tell you what those things were.
sentences.grammar: 'shall' is a formal way to say 'will' after 'I'; 'what those things were' is a noun clause.

sentences.context: In honour of my feathered friends, I have changed it from Gregg to Egg
sentences.simple: To show that I think well of the birds, I have changed my name from Gregg to Egg.
sentences.grammar: 'In honour of' starts a phrase meaning 'to show respect for'; 'have changed' is the present perfect for a change that is still true now.
